title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design Uber
summary: Design Uber at the scale of ~15 M trips/day across 10 000+ cities in 70+ countries: ride-hailing with real-time driver-rider matching, geospatial indexing (S2 / geohash), surge pricing, dispatch system, and map matching…
objectives: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design Uber at the scale of ~15 M trips/day across 10 000+ cities in 70+ countries: ride-hailing with real-time driver-rider matching, **geospatial indexing** (S2 / geohash), **surge pricing**, **dispatch system**, and **map matching** (snapping GPS to roads). Focus on the **dispatch algorithm** (find nearest driver in < 3 s), **surge pricing** (dynamic pricing based on supply/demand), and the **Kafka-based event streaming** backbone. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **Request a ride**: rider enters pickup + destination; app shows fare estimate + ETA; rider confirms.
- **Driver matching (dispatch)**: system finds the nearest available driver within ~3 s; offers the ride to that driver; if declined, offers to the next.
- **Real-time tracking**: rider sees driver location on map; driver sees rider location; both updated every 1–3 s.
- **Trip lifecycle**: request → match → driver en route → pickup → trip in progress → drop-off → payment → rating.
- **Surge pricing**: dynamic multiplier (1.0×–3.0×) based on real-time supply/demand in a geofenced area.
- **Fare calculation**: based on distance, time, base fare, surge multiplier, booking fee, tips.
- **Payments**: charge rider's payment method, pay driver (after Uber's cut).
- **Ratings**: rider rates driver, driver rates rider (1–5 stars); below 4.6 = warnings/account review.
- **Trip history**: rider and driver can view past trips.
- **Driver onboarding**: signup, background check, document verification, vehicle inspection.
- **Push notifications**: trip status updates, surge alerts, promotions.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.99% for the dispatch system (≈ 52 min downtime/year) — a missed ride = lost revenue + churn.
- **Latency**: driver match p99 < 3 s ( rider abandons after that); driver location update p99 < 500 ms; fare estimate p99 < 1 s.
- **Scale**: 15 M trips/day, ~50 M active riders, ~5 M active drivers, 10 000+ cities.
- **Throughput**: ~10 M driver location updates per minute at peak (each driver pings every 3 s); ~200 ride requests/s globally.
- **Storage**: 15 M trips/day × 10 KB metadata + 5 MB GPS track = ~75 TB/day; 1-year retention.
- **Geospatial**: must support "find nearest N drivers within radius R" in < 100 ms across 5 M drivers worldwide.
- **Consistency**: strong for trip state machine (a driver can't be matched to two riders); eventual for location (1–3 s lag OK).
- **Multi-region**: 70+ countries with regulatory isolation (data residency laws).

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Location updates**: 5 M drivers × 1 ping / 3 s = ~1.7 M pings/s globally. Each ping = 100 bytes (driver_id, lat, lon, ts, status) = 170 MB/s ingress.
- **Dispatch QPS**: 15 M trips/day ÷ 86 400 s = ~175 trips/s globally, but bursty (peak commute = 5× avg = ~875/s).
- **Geospatial index**: 5 M drivers, each in a geohash cell. To find nearest drivers in a city, scan only that city's cells — typically < 1 000 drivers. < 100 ms.
- **Trip storage**: 15 M trips/day × 5 MB GPS track = 75 TB/day → 27 PB/year. Hot 30 days → SSD; older → S3/Glacier.
- **Surge**: needs to be recomputed every 5 min per geofenced area (~1 M areas globally = ~3 300 surge updates/s).

### Scope
- **In scope**: ride request, dispatch (driver matching), surge pricing, real-time tracking, trip lifecycle, geospatial indexing, scaling.
- **Out of scope**: Uber Eats (similar dispatch but restaurant-side extra), Uber Freight, self-driving (separate R&D), full maps/routing (we use third-party like Google Maps/Mapbox), full ML for ETA (treat as black box), regulatory compliance per country (mention but don't deep-dive).

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Global DNS + Anycast** (Route 53) — routes rider/driver app to nearest regional API endpoint. 2. **API Gateway** (Envoy / Kong) — TLS, OAuth, rate limiting, request routing. Per-region deployment. 3. **Microservices** (~2 000+ services at Uber; we focus on the core): - **Rider service**: rider profile, payment methods, trip history. - **Driver service**: driver profile, vehicle, document verification, status (online/offline/busy). - **Trip service**: the state machine (requested → matched → en_route → pickup → in_progress → drop_off → completed). - **Dispatch service**: the core matching algorithm — finds nearest driver within seconds. - **Surge service**: computes dynamic pricing per geofenced area, every 5 min. - **ETA service**: predicts travel time using ML (gradient-boosted trees + road network graph). - **Pricing service**: calculates fare (base + distance + time + surge + booking fee). - **Geolocation service**: stores driver locations, supports "nearest N within radius" queries. Uses Redis GEO (geohash-backed sorted set) or Google S2 cells. - **Map matching service**: snaps noisy GPS pings to the road network graph (Hidden Markov Model). - **Payment service**: charges rider, pays driver, handles split fares. - **Notification service**: push (APNS/FCM) and SMS (Twilio) for trip updates. - **Rating service**: post-trip ratings. 4. **Geospatial index** — Redis GEO (sorted set on geohash) for driver locations; or Google S2 cell indexing in Cassandra. 5. **Kafka** — the event streaming backbone. Every state change (location update, trip status change, surge update) is an event. Consumers: ETA model, surge calculator, analytics, fraud detection. 6. **Cassandra** — trip history, GPS tracks, driver/rider profiles. Multi-region replicated. 7. **MySQL / PostgreSQL** — transactional data (payments, account balances). 8. **Redis** — geospatial index, session state, surge cache, driver status. 9. **Schema Registry** (Confluent) — Avro schemas for Kafka events. 10. **ClickHouse / Pinot** — real-time analytics (driver supply, trip volume, surge effectiveness). 11. **Mapbox / Google Maps** — third-party map tiles, routing. 12. **WebSocket gateway** — for real-time driver location streaming to the rider's app (and vice versa). ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR R([Rider App]) --> DNS[Route 53] D([Driver App]) --> DNS DNS --> GW[API Gateway / WebSocket] GW --> RSVC[Rider svc] GW --> DSVC[Driver svc] GW --> TRIP[Trip svc] GW --> DISP[Dispatch svc] GW --> LOC[Geolocation svc] GW --> WS[WebSocket gateway] WS --> R WS --> D D -->|ping every 3s| LOC LOC --> GEO[(Redis GEO
geospatial index)] R -->|request ride| TRIP TRIP --> DISP DISP --> GEO DISP --> SURGE[Surge svc] DISP --> ETA[ETA svc] DISP --> DSVC DSVC -->|offer ride| D D -->|accept| DSVC DSVC --> TRIP TRIP --> K[(Kafka: trip-events)] LOC --> K2[(Kafka: location-events)] K --> PAY[Payment svc] K --> NOTIF[Notification svc] K --> AN[(ClickHouse
analytics)] K2 --> MM[Map matching] K2 --> SURGE SURGE --> GEOF[(Redis
surge cache)] PAY --> DB[(MySQL
payments)] TRIP --> CASS[(Cassandra
trips + GPS)] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | Rider App | | Driver App | | (request ride) | | (ping every 3s) | +---+-----------+---+ +---+-----------+---+ | | | | API | | WebSocket | ping | accept v v v | +-----+-----------+----+ +------+-------+ | | API Gateway | | Geolocation | | | (per region) | | svc | | +--+--+--+--+--+--+---+ +------+-------+ | | | | | | | | | v v v v v v v | +-----+--+ ++ +-+ +++ +-----+ +-----+-----+ | |Rider| |Trip| |Dispatch| |Surge| | Redis GEO| | |svc | |svc | |svc | |svc | | (driver |<--+ +-----+ +--+-+ +---+----+ +-----+ | index) | | | +----------+ | | v v +----+--+ +--+-------+ +-----------+ |ETA svc| |Driver svc| <-----> | Driver | +-------+ +----+-----+ | accepts? | | +-----------+ v +----+----+ |Kafka: | trip-events |trip-evts|----> Payment, Notif, Analytics +---------+ +---------+ |Kafka: | location-events |loc-evts |----> Map matching, Surge +---------+ Trip lifecycle (state machine): requested -> matched -> en_route -> pickup -> in_progress -> drop_off -> completed ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Driver comes online**: Driver app `POST /api/v1/driver/online` → driver service updates status, geolocation service adds driver to Redis GEO index. From now on, driver app sends a `location_update` event every 3 s with (lat, lon, heading, speed, status). 2. **Rider requests a ride**: Rider app `POST /api/v1/trips {pickup, destination}` → trip service creates a trip in `requested` state, calls dispatch service. Trip service publishes `trip-requested` event to Kafka. 3. **Dispatch (the core algorithm)**: Dispatch service calls geolocation service → finds nearest N (say 5) available drivers within radius R (say 3 km) using Redis GEO `GEORADIUS`. For each candidate, fetches ETA from the ETA service. Sorts by ETA. Picks the closest driver. 4. **Driver offer**: Dispatch service sends a push notification to the chosen driver via WebSocket: "New ride request: 3 min away, $12.50, accept?" Driver has 15 s to accept. If declined or timeout, dispatch moves to the next candidate. 5. **Match**: Driver accepts → trip state → `matched` → `en_route`. WebSocket streams driver location to rider every 1–3 s. Driver's status → `busy` in Redis GEO (excluded from future dispatch queries). 6. **Pickup & trip**: Driver arrives → trip state → `pickup` → `in_progress`. GPS track recorded (every 3 s) to Cassandra. 7. **Drop-off**: Trip state → `drop_off` → `completed`. Payment service charges rider, pays driver. Rating prompt sent. 8. **Surge**: Continuously (every 5 min per geofenced area), surge service consumes `trip-requested` and `driver-online` events from Kafka, computes the supply/demand ratio, and updates the surge multiplier in Redis. Pricing service uses this multiplier for fare estimates.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**Cassandra — `trips` (trip metadata)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE trips (
    trip_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    rider_id       UUID,
    driver_id      UUID,
    pickup_lat     DOUBLE,
    pickup_lon     DOUBLE,
    dest_lat       DOUBLE,
    dest_lon       DOUBLE,
    status         TEXT,            -- requested | matched | en_route | pickup | in_progress | drop_off | completed | canceled
    surge_mult     DOUBLE,
    fare           DECIMAL,
    distance_m     INT,
    duration_s     INT,
    requested_at   TIMESTAMP,
    completed_at   TIMESTAMP
);
```

**Cassandra — `trip_locations` (GPS track, time-series)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE trip_locations (
    trip_id     UUID,
    ts          TIMESTAMP,
    lat         DOUBLE,
    lon         DOUBLE,
    heading     DOUBLE,           -- degrees 0-360
    speed       DOUBLE,           -- m/s
    PRIMARY KEY (trip_id, ts)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts ASC);
```

**Cassandra — `driver_locations` (current driver position, hot)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE driver_locations (
    driver_id   UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    lat         DOUBLE,
    lon         DOUBLE,
    heading     DOUBLE,
    speed       DOUBLE,
    status      TEXT,             -- online | busy | offline
    updated_at  TIMESTAMP
);
```

**PostgreSQL — `riders`, `drivers`, `payments`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE riders (
    rider_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    name          VARCHAR(100),
    email         VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE,
    phone         VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE,
    rating        DECIMAL(2,1),    -- 4.7 avg
    payment_method JSONB,          -- {type: card, token: ...}
    created_at    TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE drivers (
    driver_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    name          VARCHAR(100),
    email         VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE,
    phone         VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE,
    rating        DECIMAL(2,1),
    vehicle_make  VARCHAR(50),
    vehicle_model VARCHAR(50),
    license_plate VARCHAR(20),
    background_check_status TEXT,  -- pending | passed | failed
    onboarded_at  TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id    UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    trip_id       UUID,
    rider_id      UUID,
    driver_id     UUID,
    amount        DECIMAL(10,2),
    currency      VARCHAR(3),
    status        TEXT,            -- pending | captured | refunded | failed
    created_at    TIMESTAMP
);
```

**Redis — geospatial index (driver locations)**
```
GEOADD drivers:online  {lon} {lat} {driver_id}
GEORADIUS drivers:online  {lon} {lat} 3 km COUNT 5 ASC
   -> returns nearest 5 driver_ids within 3 km, sorted by distance
```

**Redis — driver status (separate from GEO index)**
```
SET driver_status:{driver_id}  online | busy | offline
EXPIRE driver_status:{driver_id} 30   # if no ping in 30s, marked offline
```

**Redis — surge multipliers (per geofenced area)**
```
SET surge:{geohash6}  1.5   # 1.5x surge in this area
EXPIRE surge:{geohash6} 600 # 10-minute TTL
```

### Indexes
- Cassandra `trips`: PRIMARY KEY on `trip_id`; secondary index on `rider_id` and `driver_id` for "show me my trips."
- Cassandra `trip_locations`: PRIMARY KEY `(trip_id, ts ASC)` — natural time-series scan.
- Cassandra `driver_locations`: PRIMARY KEY on `driver_id` — direct lookup.
- PostgreSQL: unique index on email/phone; index on `trip_id` for payments.
- Redis GEO: sorted set on geohash — supports `GEORADIUS` for nearest-N queries.
- S2 cell index (optional): drivers indexed by S2 cell ID at level 12 (~3 km² cells). Supports "all drivers in this cell" lookups.

### Storage Choice
- **Cassandra** for trips, GPS tracks, driver locations — write-heavy, time-series, multi-region.
- **PostgreSQL** for transactional data (payments, accounts) — strong consistency required.
- **Redis GEO** for the geospatial index — sub-ms nearest-N queries; in-memory.
- **Kafka** for the event backbone — durable, partitioned, replayable.
- **ClickHouse / Pinot** for analytics — columnar, fast aggregations on billions of trips.
- **S3** for cold trip storage (> 1 year) — cheap, durable, for compliance/legal retention.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Find the nearest available driver and offer the ride.
- Compute surge multiplier for a geohash cell.
- Look up the surge multiplier for a location.
- Simplified map matching using a Hidden Markov Model (HMM).
- Driver comes online / goes offline
- Driver location update (every 3s, via WebSocket or HTTP)
- Rider requests a ride
- Driver accepts / declines a ride offer

**Defines:** `dispatch_trip()`, `compute_surge_for_cell()`, `get_surge_for_location()`, `haversine_m()`, `map_match()`

### API Design
```
# Driver comes online / goes offline
POST   /api/v1/driver/online
POST   /api/v1/driver/offline

# Driver location update (every 3s, via WebSocket or HTTP)
POST   /api/v1/driver/location
       { lat, lon, heading, speed }

# Rider requests a ride
POST   /api/v1/trips
       { pickup, destination, ride_type }
       -> 201 Created { trip_id, status: requested }

# Get trip status
GET    /api/v1/trips/{trip_id}
       -> 200 OK { status, driver, eta, fare_estimate }

# Driver accepts / declines a ride offer
POST   /api/v1/trips/{trip_id}/accept
POST   /api/v1/trips/{trip_id}/decline

# Update trip state (driver only)
POST   /api/v1/trips/{trip_id}/state
       { state: en_route | pickup | in_progress | drop_off | completed }

# Fare estimate (before requesting)
GET    /api/v1/fare-estimate?pickup=...&dest=...
       -> 200 OK { fare_low, fare_high, eta, surge_mult }

# Trip history
GET    /api/v1/trips/history?user_id=...&limit=20

# Rating (after trip)
POST   /api/v1/trips/{trip_id}/rating
       { rating: 5, comment: "great driver" }
```

### Key Algorithms

#### (1) Dispatch — find nearest driver within seconds

```python
import redis, time

REDIS = redis.Redis(host='geo-redis-cluster', port=6379)
DRIVER_OFFER_TIMEOUT_S = 15   # driver has 15s to accept
SEARCH_RADIUS_KM       = 3
MAX_CANDIDATES         = 10

def dispatch_trip(trip_id: str, pickup_lat: float, pickup_lon: float):
    """Find the nearest available driver and offer the ride."""
    # 1. Query Redis GEO for nearest drivers within radius
    candidates = REDIS.georadius(
        'drivers:online',
        longitude=pickup_lon, latitude=pickup_lat,
        radius=SEARCH_RADIUS_KM, unit='km',
        withdist=True, withcoord=True,
        count=MAX_CANDIDATES, sort='ASC'
    )
    # candidates = [(driver_id, distance_km, (lon, lat)), ...]

    # 2. Filter out busy drivers (their status is updated on accept)
    available = []
    for driver_id, dist, coord in candidates:
        status = REDIS.get(f"driver_status:{driver_id}")
        if status == b'online':
            available.append((driver_id, dist, coord))

    if not available:
        # No drivers nearby -> increase radius and retry, or queue
        return {"status": "no_drivers_available", "trip_id": trip_id}

    # 3. For each candidate, fetch ETA (driving time, not straight-line)
    for driver_id, dist, coord in available:
        eta_seconds = eta_service.predict(
            (coord[1], coord[0]),   # driver lat/lon
            (pickup_lat, pickup_lon),
        )
        # 4. Offer the ride via WebSocket push to driver
        offer = {
            "trip_id": trip_id,
            "pickup_lat": pickup_lat,
            "pickup_lon": pickup_lon,
            "eta_to_pickup_s": eta_seconds,
            "fare_estimate": pricing_service.estimate(trip_id),
            "expires_at": time.time() + DRIVER_OFFER_TIMEOUT_S,
        }
        websocket.send_to_driver(driver_id, {"type": "ride_offer", **offer})

        # 5. Wait for driver response (with timeout)
        response = wait_for_driver_response(driver_id, trip_id,
                                             timeout=DRIVER_OFFER_TIMEOUT_S)
        if response == "accept":
            # 6. Mark driver busy, transition trip to matched
            REDIS.set(f"driver_status:{driver_id}", "busy")
            REDIS.zrem("drivers:online", driver_id)   # remove from GEO index
            trip_service.update_state(trip_id, "matched",
                                       driver_id=driver_id)
            return {"status": "matched", "driver_id": driver_id,
                    "eta_s": eta_seconds}
        # else: timeout or decline -> try next candidate

    # 7. All candidates declined -> expand radius and retry
    return dispatch_trip(trip_id, pickup_lat, pickup_lon)  # recursive retry with larger radius
```

#### (2) Surge pricing — supply/demand ratio per geofenced area

```python
import geohash, time

GEOHASH_PRECISION = 6     # ~1.2km x 0.6km cells
SURGE_MAX         = 3.0
SURGE_MIN         = 1.0
SURGE_WINDOW_S    = 300   # 5-minute rolling window
SURGE_UPDATE_S    = 60    # recompute every 60s

def compute_surge_for_cell(cell: str):
    """Compute surge multiplier for a geohash cell."""
    # 1. Count open ride requests in this cell in last 5 min (demand)
    demand = kafka_consumer.count_events(
        topic="trip-requested",
        filter=lambda e: geohash.encode(e.pickup_lat, e.pickup_lon, GEOHASH_PRECISION) == cell,
        window_s=SURGE_WINDOW_S,
    )

    # 2. Count available drivers in this cell (supply)
    supply = redis.georadius("drivers:online",
                              *geohash.decode(cell),
                              radius=0.6, unit='km',  # cell is ~1.2km wide
                              count=10000)            # all drivers
    supply_count = len(supply)

    # 3. Compute supply/demand ratio
    if demand == 0:
        surge = SURGE_MIN
    else:
        ratio = supply_count / demand
        # Higher ratio -> lower surge (plenty of supply)
        # Lower ratio  -> higher surge (scarcity)
        surge = max(SURGE_MIN, min(SURGE_MAX, 1.5 / max(ratio, 0.1)))

    # 4. Round to nearest 0.1 (surge is shown as 1.2x, 1.5x, etc.)
    surge = round(surge * 10) / 10

    # 5. Cache in Redis with TTL
    redis.setex(f"surge:{cell}", SURGE_UPDATE_S * 2, surge)
    return surge

def get_surge_for_location(lat: float, lon: float) -> float:
    """Look up the surge multiplier for a location."""
    cell = geohash.encode(lat, lon, GEOHASH_PRECISION)
    surge = redis.get(f"surge:{cell}")
    if surge is None:
        # Cell not cached -> compute on demand (rare)
        surge = compute_surge_for_cell(cell)
    return float(surge)
```

#### (3) Map matching — snap noisy GPS to the road network

```python
"""Simplified map matching using a Hidden Markov Model (HMM).
Uber uses a similar approach (based on the Newson & Krumm 2009 paper)."""

import math

def haversine_m(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) -> float:
    """Distance in meters between two GPS points."""
    R = 6371000  # Earth radius in meters
    p = math.pi / 180
    a = (0.5 - math.cos((lat2-lat1)*p)/2 +
         math.cos(lat1*p) * math.cos(lat2*p) *
         (1 - math.cos((lon2-lon1)*p)) / 2)
    return 2 * R * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))

def map_match(gps_pings: list, road_network: RoadNetwork) -> list:
    """Snap a sequence of GPS pings to the most likely road path.

    HMM:
      - states = road segments (edges in the graph)
      - observations = GPS pings
      - transition prob = 1 / exp(-distance_diff / beta)  (Newson & Krumm)
      - emission prob   = 1 / exp(-gps_to_road_distance / sigma)
    """
    # 1. For each GPS ping, find candidate road segments within 50m
    candidates_per_ping = []
    for ping in gps_pings:
        nearby_roads = road_network.query(ping.lat, ping.lon, radius_m=50)
        candidates_per_ping.append(nearby_roads)

    # 2. Viterbi algorithm to find the most likely sequence of road segments
    V = [{}]  # V[t][road_id] = (prob, backpointer)
    for road in candidates_per_ping[0]:
        # Emission probability: closer road = higher prob
        d = haversine_m(gps_pings[0].lat, gps_pings[0].lon,
                         road.lat, road.lon)
        V[0][road.id] = (math.exp(-d / 20.0), None)   # sigma = 20m

    for t in range(1, len(gps_pings)):
        V.append({})
        for curr_road in candidates_per_ping[t]:
            best_prob, best_prev = 0, None
            for prev_road_id, (prev_prob, _) in V[t-1].items():
                prev_road = road_network.get(prev_road_id)
                # Transition: difference between GPS distance and road-network distance
                gps_d = haversine_m(gps_pings[t-1].lat, gps_pings[t-1].lon,
                                     gps_pings[t].lat, gps_pings[t].lon)
                road_d = road_network.path_distance(prev_road, curr_road)
                transition = math.exp(-abs(gps_d - road_d) / 50.0)  # beta = 50m
                # Emission
                d = haversine_m(gps_pings[t].lat, gps_pings[t].lon,
                                 curr_road.lat, curr_road.lon)
                emission = math.exp(-d / 20.0)
                prob = prev_prob * transition * emission
                if prob > best_prob:
                    best_prob, best_prev = prob, prev_road_id
            V[t][curr_road.id] = (best_prob, best_prev)

    # 3. Backtrack to find the best path
    best_final = max(V[-1], key=lambda r: V[-1][r][0])
    path = [best_final]
    for t in range(len(V)-1, 0, -1):
        best_final = V[t][best_final][1]
        path.append(best_final)
    path.reverse()
    return path
```

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **1.7 M driver location updates/s globally**: each ping = 100 bytes, but the geospatial index must reflect reality within 3 s. Solution: shard Redis GEO by region (US-East, EU-West, etc.); use Redis Cluster for horizontal scaling; update Redis directly from the WebSocket gateway (skip the API server hop).
- **Dispatch latency < 3 s**: dispatch involves a Redis query, ETA model call, WebSocket push to driver, and 15-s driver timeout. Solution: pre-fetch ETAs for top candidates in parallel; pipeline the Redis and ETA calls.
- **Surge computation at scale**: 1 M geofenced cells × 5-min recomputation = 3 300 surge updates/s. Solution: Flink streaming job consumes `trip-requested` and `driver-online` events, maintains per-cell rolling counts in memory, emits surge updates every 5 min.
- **Multi-region data residency**: EU data must stay in EU (GDPR); China data must stay in China. Solution: per-region deployment with isolated databases; cross-region replication only for non-PII data (analytics).
- **Driver status consistency**: a driver can't be matched to two riders. Solution: Redis atomic `SETNX` (set if not exists) on `driver_status:{id} = busy` — only the first match wins; subsequent dispatch queries skip busy drivers.
- **Trip state machine integrity**: trips must transition through valid states only. Solution: a state machine service with strict transition validation; invalid transitions rejected.

### Caching Strategy
- **L1 — Redis GEO**: driver locations. Updated on every ping (3 s). No TTL (driver is removed on offline).
- **L2 — Redis surge cache**: surge multipliers per cell. TTL 10 min (refreshed every 5 min).
- **L3 — Redis driver status**: online/busy/offline. TTL 30 s (auto-offline if no ping).
- **L4 — Redis ETA cache**: ETA for common (pickup, dest) pairs. TTL 5 min.
- **L5 — Redis fare estimate cache**: per (pickup, dest, ride_type). TTL 1 min.
- **L6 — CDN (for static assets)**: app binaries, map tiles (via Mapbox/Google).

### Failure Modes
| Failure | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Redis GEO cluster down | Dispatch breaks (can't find drivers) | Multi-AZ Redis Cluster with failover; fallback to Cassandra S2 cell index (slower but available) |
| WebSocket gateway failure | Rider/driver can't see real-time updates | Multiple WebSocket gateways per region; client reconnects to a healthy one |
| Kafka broker down | Some events delayed or lost | Multi-broker RF=3; consumers commit offset only after Cassandra write |
| Driver app loses connection | Driver appears "stuck" at old location | 30-s TTL on driver_status auto-marks offline; driver re-pings on reconnect |
| Surge service down | Pricing uses stale surge (cached 10 min) | Surge cache TTL 10 min absorbs outage; pricing service falls back to last-known multiplier |
| ETA service timeout | Dispatch falls back to straight-line distance | Dispatch has 200 ms timeout for ETA; on timeout, uses haversine distance (less accurate but works) |
| Payment service down | Rider can't complete trip | Trip can end (state → completed); payment is queued and processed when service recovers |
| Driver accepts but doesn't show up | Rider stranded | Auto-cancel after 5 min of no movement; offer next driver |
| GPS spoofing (driver or rider) | Fraud: driver pretends to be at pickup | Map matching detects jumps > 200 m in 3 s; flag for fraud review |
| Multi-region failover needed (e.g., AWS region outage) | Region's trips fail | Active-active per-region; Route 53 fails over API to a neighbor region; trips in progress complete locally |
